snippets.snippet_text: The Hebrew word chazon ('vision') is not a casual sight or private dream but a formally received divine communication—a revelatory disclosure in which God opens the prophet's perception to spiritual realities. This vision form parallels the temple endowment, where covenants are enacted visually and symbolically.

God's indictment reaches its climax with a stunning claim: He is 'full' (glutted, satiated to disgust) with their sacrifices and offerings. This is not rejection of the sacrificial system itself, but of sacrifices offered by those living unjustly—a principle that D&C 97:8 makes clear applies to modern temples as well.

After devastating accusations, God suddenly shifts tone: 'Come now, let us reason together' (lechu na venivvakhechah). The Hebrew implies God is inviting Israel to settle a dispute, not as a defeated opponent but as a parent reasoning with a wayward child—a model of divine justice that anticipates the temple experience of standing before God.

Though your sins are scarlet, they shall become white as snow—Isaiah's promise of complete restoration through divine refining. This metallurgical image parallels Malachi's 'refiner's fire' language, central to Latter-day Saint understanding of how temple covenants strip away impurities and refine the soul.

Zion's redemption will be achieved not apart from judgment but through it—salvation and justice are unified, not opposed. This radical claim (Isaiah 1:27) reshapes how we understand temple covenants: the stripping away and humiliation are not separate from salvation but constitute its very pathway.

On the Day of the LORD, every human exaltation will be brought low—cedars of Lebanon, high mountains, fortified towers, and merchant ships will all be humbled. The principle is absolute: human pride and divine exaltation are mutually exclusive. This foundational claim (Isaiah 2:11-17) structures all biblical eschatology and the temple's teaching on human accountability.
